title: The Iowa Corridor
text:
The contract posted at 04:40, while the <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a927-73ac-abfa-37c77f9cff8d">GLMZ</entity> was still deciding whether the dark was done.

TASK: FREIGHT ESCORT — SEED STOCK CONSIGNMENT (AGRICULTURAL, PERISHABLE).
ROUTE: <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a927-73ac-abfa-37c77f9cff8d">GLMZ</entity> FRINGE → CEDAR RAPIDS DEPOT, CEDAR RAPIDS TERRITORY.
TRANSIT: IOWA CORRIDOR — BEHEMOTH OPERATIONAL ZONE, ACTIVE SCHEDULE.
CREW CONFIRMED: RIA (DRIVE), GANTRY (RIGGING), KYLE (SECURITY).
BEHEMOTH NAVIGATION ADVISORY: CLIENT WILL ISSUE IN-TRANSIT.
STANDARD RATE. FUEL AND TOLLS BILLED AT COST.
ADDENDUM: BRING SNACKS. THE HAUL IS EIGHT HOURS.

<entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity> had taken the contract because she needed the <entity repo="material" guid="d6cc00f6-2360-9a5d-5f6c-3a1996617b06">Cedar</entity> Rapids run on her corridor record before the quarter closed — one more logged transit through an active Behemoth zone and she could apply for the Tier Two hauler certification that had been sitting just out of reach for eleven months. Eight hours, standard rate, and a stamp on her record. That was the whole calculation, and she'd said it to <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> like a woman reciting a thing she'd already recited to herself forty times: *one clean run, that's all this is.*

<entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity> was already at the hauler when <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> arrived — a blunt-nosed cargo rig with sponsorship logos running down its flanks. The chromatophore panels on her legs cycled <entity repo="corponation" guid="019d6143-a7aa-7ce2-8a57-5b78e5c63d88">Ferrogate Transit</entity>'s sunrise campaign at one-quarter brightness, which was her entire opinion of <entity repo="corponation" guid="019d6143-a7aa-7ce2-8a57-5b78e5c63d88">Ferrogate Transit</entity>. She had the cargo manifest in one hand and a thermos in the other and the look of a woman who had done this run twice and was getting paid to do it again.

"Fourteen crates," she said, by way of greeting. "Thirty-two varieties of heritage soy, two of nitrogen-fixing legume, and one the manifest calls experimental, the shipper calls proprietary, and I call not-my-problem-until-it-becomes-my-problem."

"Does the experimental crate make noise?"

"Not yet."

"Then it's not yet your problem."

She handed him the thermos, which meant she'd brought it to share. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> took one mouthful — pu-erh that had been steeping since before either of them was up — and handed it back without comment. The thermos was not payment, so he could take it.

<entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-6eb0-7176-9136-790a0ed124fb">Gantry</entity> was already up on the flatbed frame, checking strap tension on the cargo pallet with the focus of someone who knew things could move. She was about six feet of quiet in a rigger's coat. She spent words the way some people spent money: carefully, and only when the thing was worth it. Right now she was spending none. She was talking to the load straps instead, low, second person, the way some haulers talk to a questionable weld — not sure it can hear them, not willing to bet the load that it can't.

"Anything shifting?" <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> asked.

"Not yet," <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-6eb0-7176-9136-790a0ed124fb">Gantry</entity> said. Two words.

They pulled out of the <entity repo="corponation" guid="019d6143-a7a5-7dfd-8f9f-91502211ef14">Ashgrave</entity> fringe at 05:15. The hauler's engine did its honest work, and the city folded away behind them in layers, tier by tier, until the last one dropped below sight. Then there was just the elevated causeway, the pre-dawn brown of open sky, and the flat country starting to assert itself past the ferrocement boundary wall.

The corridor checkpoint at the wall was where the run stopped being simple. <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity> brought the hauler down to a crawl and thumbed her certification chip against the reader, expecting the same green wash she'd gotten twice before. Instead the panel went amber and held, and the checkpoint officer leaned out of his booth with the unhurried expression of a man about to ruin someone's quarter.

"Behemoth advisory came down at oh-five-hundred," he said. "<entity repo="material" guid="d6cc00f6-2360-9a5d-5f6c-3a1996617b06">Cedar</entity> Rapids corridor's been reclassified to restricted schedule as of this morning. Active zone transits are provisional-hold pending client-issued navigation windows." He tapped something <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity> couldn't see. "Which means your logged transit doesn't log — not as a clean run. It'll flag as provisional on your record. Provisional doesn't count toward Tier Two."

"It counted last week."

"Last week the schedule was open." He shrugged, not unkindly. "You can still run it. Cargo's perishable, client's expecting it, and I've got no cause to hold you. But if you want this on your certification you'll need a clean-transit variance, and those come from the client's navigation officer — the one who hasn't issued your window yet. In-transit, per your own contract." He handed the chip back through the slot. "So you're driving eight hours toward a stamp that a stranger somewhere ahead of you may or may not decide to sign off on."

<entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity>'s hand closed around the chip a beat too hard. Eleven months of provisional runs, of almost, of *next quarter*, and the answer had never once been *no* — it had always been a door that stayed shut for reasons that lived somewhere she couldn't see, decided by somebody she couldn't argue with. She'd done everything right. She'd logged every hour. It had never once been enough on its own.

"Course it does," she said, flat, and pocketed the chip like it had personally offended her.

Behind her, the experimental crate chose that moment to make a sound — a low, settling groan of stressed casing that hadn't been there a minute ago.

"That's new," <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-6eb0-7176-9136-790a0ed124fb">Gantry</entity> said. Two words, and a hand already going to the straps.

<entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-6eb0-7176-9136-790a0ed124fb">Gantry</entity> had the strap tight and the crate quiet inside forty seconds, which told <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> something about how many times she'd done this exact motion for cargo that had never once asked permission to shift. She didn't look up when she was done. She just went back to not-talking to the load.

The <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aabb-7370-8444-839d7f7bc429">Iowa</entity> corridor started at the wall's west service gate, which cost <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity> a Φ45 transit stamp and a seven-minute argument with a gate officer about whether "perishable agricultural" covered "experimental proprietary" on the same manifest.

It did not. It cost Φ8 extra.

"Logged," <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity> said, making a note in her overlay, "as a cost of goods." She drove through the gate without looking back at it, the way you don't look back at a toll booth that's already taken your money — nothing left there to want.

Past the wall, the land opened in a way that had no equal in the <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a927-73ac-abfa-37c77f9cff8d">GLMZ</entity>. The hauler's elevation sensors counted down from the city's sixteenth-floor surface baseline to something like ground — actual ground, the old kind with no building underneath it — and the sky became an impossible amount of sky. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> sat in the cab's jump seat and watched it arrive.

The terminal in his coat chirped.

CLIENT ADVISES: THIS SEGMENT IS OWNED SCHEDULE, NOT OPEN ROAD.
CLIENT ADVISES: DO NOT DEVIATE FROM POSTED WAYPOINTS.
CLIENT ADVISES: IF CLIENT POSTS STOP — STOP. DO NOT ASK.
ADDENDUM: THE HAULER'S CARGO IS WORTH MORE THAN THE HAULER. DRIVE ACCORDINGLY.

"Your client is posting," <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity> said.

"It's navigating."

"It's navigating us through <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aabb-7370-8444-839d7f7bc429">Iowa</entity>." She glanced at him over the center console. "How does it have Behemoth schedules? The advisory only came down at oh-five-hundred. Nobody's supposed to have a live picture of drift patterns this far out — that's classified above corridor-officer pay grade, and corridor officers are the ones who told me *no.*"

"Ask it," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "It charges for answers, though."

<entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity> looked up at the cab ceiling, the way you look at the sky when you want it to tell you something, and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> watched her run the actual arithmetic behind the joke: what a question costs when you're already three tolls and a provisional stamp into a quarter you can't afford to lose twice. She had eleven months of *almost* riding on this run. She could not also spend money finding out why the thing steering them through it knew more than the wall did.

"Never mind," she said. "I'll drive."

She said it the way she'd pocketed the chip — flat, decided, a door closing on her own hand before someone else could close it for her. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> filed the wrongness of it next to the rest of what he couldn't source: the client's certainty, the too-clean schedule, the shape of an authority that answered to nobody's checkpoint but its own.

The terminal chirped again.

WAYPOINT ONE IN NINE MINUTES. HOLD LANE.

The first Behemoth appeared at mile marker 27, and appeared is the right word. It didn't come from somewhere. It resolved out of the middle distance the way a weather system does — a wrongness in the grain of the prairie before it was a shape at all — until you had to accept that the scale was real and the flat land was not so flat.

It was a harvester-process unit, one of the <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aabb-7370-8444-839d7f7bc429">Iowa</entity> Cooperative's agricultural fleet. Two hundred sixty feet at the shoulder. Track width wider than the causeway. A processing tower along its back venting steam in columns the height of office buildings. It ran a parallel course a mile east, moving at the pace of something that had no idea of urgency and had never needed one. A building that had decided to walk.

<entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-6eb0-7176-9136-790a0ed124fb">Gantry</entity>, visible through the cab's rear window, watched it with the stillness of someone resetting the scale of what the world could hold.

"That's a Behemoth," <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity> said.

"Yes," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

"I've seen photos."

"Photos are wrong," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

The terminal chirped.

CLIENT ADVISES: STOP.
WAIT 214 SECONDS.
DO NOT ASK.

<entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity> brought the hauler to a full halt, engine idling too loud now in the cab. The next waypoint was thirty feet ahead. Whatever the window was, the entity had measured it to the second — and being a second early or a second late would be the entity's problem only if it chose to say why.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> counted anyway. One hundred and four. One hundred and five. The harvester's cutting heads rotated in sequence, a rhythm like breathing, like the thing was inhaling the ground and exhaling emptiness. Behind them <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-6eb0-7176-9136-790a0ed124fb">Gantry</entity>'s hand had found the door frame.

At second 214, a second Behemoth crossed their line of travel two hundred yards ahead — perpendicular, heading south, a combine-and-sort unit on its own errand. The ground came up through <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s boots before the sound did, a mechanical thrum his neuretics read as seismic, equipment-grade, no threat. Close enough to see the dust caked in its joints, the wear on its plates, the industrial precision of how it moved — no hesitation, no variation, a machine executing instructions with the confidence of something that had never once been told no. The vents fired, the plume went straight up, and the hauler's windows flexed in the pressure wave.

They sat quiet until it passed.

"Okay," <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity> said, at some point after. She put the hauler back in drive.

The terminal chirped again, and this time it did not advise. CLIENT WITHDRAWS ROUTE AUTHORITY. WINDOW CLOSED. RECALCULATING. Then, below it, a second line that hadn't been there before, hadn't been part of any briefing: SECONDARY CROSSING NOT ANTICIPATED. The combine-and-sort unit had not been on the entity's map. Something had moved that the thing steering them could not see — and for the space of the plume clearing, the hauler had been sitting exactly where the entity had promised nothing would be.

<entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity>'s hand stayed on the drive selector without pushing it forward.

"It didn't know about the second one?" she asked.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> looked at the terminal, then at the flat land that was not flat, and did not say anything, because there was nothing to say that made the silence on the screen mean less than it meant.

They stopped for fuel at a waypoint depot. The woman who ran it was named Paz. She kept three lumen mice in a cage behind the counter, and they threw a thin blue light across her hands while she worked the register. She charged Φ11 a liter for diesel. That was gouging, but the middle of <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aabb-7370-8444-839d7f7bc429">Iowa</entity> had earned the right to gouge — you don't run a pump station three hundred miles from anywhere out of the goodness of your heart. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> paid it. Paz threw in a bag of dried apples and didn't mention it. It was the prairie's version of <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity>'s fish ball, and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> took it on the same terms: with a nod and no thanks, because thanking it would have made it a transaction instead of a kindness.

<entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-6eb0-7176-9136-790a0ed124fb">Gantry</entity> was down from the rig before the engine finished cycling off, moving with the economy of someone who had already calculated the exact path to the cargo straps. She rechecked them while the fuel ran — lines that had been tight forty minutes ago and were still tight now, but the checking was its own language. She spent about twelve of her daily words on the pallet. <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity> watched from the driver's door.

"She does that every run," <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity> said.

"The cargo holds," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

"Yes," she said. "She seems comfortable with the question."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> wanted to be back on the road inside ten minutes — top off the tank, verify the straps, and roll before the crossing window slipped past. Nothing here was worth lingering over.

The terminal chirped.

CLIENT ADVISES: RIVER CROSSING — MILE MARKER 116. MUNICIPAL TOLL: Φ4. ADVISORY ONLY.
CLIENT ADVISES: THREE-HOUR WINDOW OPENS IN FORTY MINUTES. WAYPOINT 7 APPROACH TIMED FOR WINDOW.
ADDENDUM: THE EXPERIMENTAL CRATE IS FINE. NITROGEN-FIXERS USUALLY ARE. CLIENT HAS REVIEWED THE PROTOCOL DOCUMENTATION.

"Tell your client I didn't ask about the crate," <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity> said.

"It knew you were thinking about it."

"That's not better," she said.

Mile marker 74 was not on the schedule.

The terminal had posted a new waypoint — a maintenance detour — and <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity> had followed it west onto a secondary haul road. Then the Behemoth was just there. Not moving. Stopped in its own repair cycle, one track taken apart on the ground in segments, a maintenance crane working its middle. It filled the near distance the way a mountain does. Completely. No apology for it.

Close enough to count rivets. Close enough that the cab's outside sensors logged the air rising two degrees off its heat. Close enough that the ground-shake came up through the frame and the jump seat and into their spines before they heard a sound.

<entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity> brought the hauler down to a crawl. Not a stop. The waypoint said keep moving, and the waypoint was the only map they had.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said nothing. There was no one to ask.

<entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-6eb0-7176-9136-790a0ed124fb">Gantry</entity> had thirty-eight words left for the day and spent none of them. She was at the cab's rear window, both hands on the frame, watching.

The crane swung through an arc with a part the size of a shipping container at the end of it. It moved without strain — a thing heavy enough that nothing but its own weight decided where it went. On the platform hung from its shoulder joint, two figures worked, small as a postage stamp against the body's scale, moving with the deliberate slowness of people doing something that mattered. The vents fired. A column of steam climbed. The crane swung back. The Behemoth's sensor housing, itself as big as the hauler, turned a few degrees and pointed somewhere else — north, toward the horizon, at something at its own scale. They were beneath its notice, the way the bag of dried apples had been.

Somewhere in the back, a hand found a sleeve.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> did not look to see whose.

They drove past at walking speed, into the shadow the Behemoth threw across the road, dark enough that the cab's instrument lights came up on their own. The engine was the smallest sound in the world. When the road curved away and the Behemoth shrank to the size of a building, then to the size of a thought, <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity> let out a breath she'd been holding for a few hundred feet.

"Right," she said.

That was the whole review.

Kilometer 187 was the river crossing, and the toll was not the problem.

The hauler was thirty feet onto the bridge when the winch-rig came up out of the drainage cut on <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a93d-7375-a7fb-c2f162bba487">the east bank</entity>. A salvage crane on a flatbed, cable-spool running, a bolt-thrower on each side, a crew of four who had worked this choke point long enough to stop being nervous about it. It was a good spot. The bridge squeezed everything into a six-foot lane, and the crane's arm reached the whole span. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> took it in at a glance: maybe Φ800 of field-modified gear, and a forged permit that had cost less than the paint on the crane.

Their spotter was up on the upstream support, walking-stick grip, inverted, and that was what made the choke point work. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> clocked him and clocked something else in the same half-second — a shape in the drainage cut's shadow that didn't belong to the toll crew's headcount. Small. Crouched wrong for an adult. He filed it and kept his hands where the toll crew could see them, because two problems solved out of order was still two problems.

<entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity> had already stopped the hauler, both hands on the wheel, no theater in it. She'd run freight long enough to know which moves read clean.

The crane operator came to the driver's window with a bolt-thrower slung over one shoulder like a prop he'd had a long time, and threw a right-of-way notice up between them. The letterhead was right. The stamp was wrong.

"<entity repo="character" guid="019e9e4f-183b-7977-b5ab-a0260fcb4086">River</entity> bridge toll," he said. "Non-standard approach, right of way purchased from the county. Φ45 per axle." He rattled it off like a man who did it daily. "Your rig's got four drive axles. That's one hundred eighty Φ, plus equipment surcharge on the cargo."

"That permit's forged," <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity> said.

"That's a big claim."

The terminal chirped.

CLIENT ADVISES: THE RIGHT-OF-WAY REGISTRATION NUMBER ON THAT DOCUMENT DOES NOT EXIST.
CLIENT ADVISES: REAL COUNTY CROSSING FEE IS Φ4 FLAT.
CLIENT ADVISES: THE WINCH DRUM IS THE PROBLEM.
ADDENDUM: KYLE.

Six in <entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">the cylinder</entity>. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> pulled <entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">Cacophony</entity>.

He shot the winch drum at the base of the crane. Once. The round punched through it at the bearing housing and the cable-spool opened clean, the cable running free in a long clatter across the bridge deck. Then he was out of the cab, because the throwers were swinging and a parked cab was a bad answer to two bolt-throwers.

One spent. Five left.

The nearer thrower had a power-cell housing at the grip — not load-bearing, which made it a seam. <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> found it. The launcher went from a working weapon to a paperweight, about Φ180 of crane hardware calling itself a total loss. The operator backed off with the look of a man rethinking the whole trade.

That was when the shape from the drainage cut moved, and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s read on the day went from bad to worse.

She came up the embankment fast and low, cutting the angle toward the crane's control housing instead of away from the fight — toward the machine, not away from it, which was exactly backward from what anyone smart would do with two armed men still upright. Fourteen years old. Good boots, bad judgment, a courier satchel bouncing against her hip that had no business anywhere near a toll ambush.

"<entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity>—" <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> got half her name out before the second thrower's operator saw her too, and swung wide of <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> to bring the weapon to bear on the smaller, closer target, because that was the math an untrained eye did under pressure — the thing that moves fastest is the thing that scares you most.

The bolt took a chunk out of the crane's own housing eighteen inches from her head. Close enough that the report of it walked her whole balance sideways. She went down on one knee behind a hydraulic strut, not because it was cover — because it was the only thing there.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s ribs told him about the next three feet before he'd covered them. He closed the distance anyway and put himself between the thrower's second angle and the strut, <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> already moving, and took the operator's wrist off the weapon's grip with the flat of <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity> instead of the edge, because there wasn't time to decide whether the man deserved the edge and there wasn't time not to decide either. The thrower clattered to the deck. The man went down holding his arm to his chest, more surprised than hurt.

<entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-6eb0-7176-9136-790a0ed124fb">Gantry</entity> had the crane's counterweight already — she'd been watching it since the flatbed showed up, the way riggers watch these things, quietly and well before anyone else needed her to. A steel box the size of a man's torso, chained above the winch. She spent five of her words on it.

"That's going to fall."

The operator looked at the counterweight, looked at where it was headed — straight down onto his own winch — and used his four seconds well. He was ten feet clear when it hit. The winch went flat with the sound of something heavy deciding the conversation was over, cable tangled past saving, and the toll operation became a piece of debris blocking a bridge in the space of one second.

The spotter climbed down off the strut with nothing left to add. "We're done. Bridge is yours."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> didn't watch him go. He was already crouched at the strut, one hand under <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity>'s arm, hauling her up onto feet that weren't quite steady yet.

"You were in the drainage cut," he said. Flat. The read-out voice, the one he used on scared kids, except he wasn't sure yet which of them it was for.

"I was tracking the spotter since mile marker one-fourteen." Her voice came out fast, professional, running ahead of whatever was happening in her chest. "Off the hauler's rear camera. I climbed out at the fuel stop, I wanted to see the crossing—"
